appraisal_events.evidence: Her attention snaps tight whenever Charlus is named (« la Princesse reprenait en mains les rênes détendues de son attention »), her defence of « un homme de l'immense valeur de Palamède » betrays « ce qu'elle cherchait à magnifier », and the coach episode ends with « Devenant subitement très rouge, elle me donna la lettre », addressed to M. de Charlus.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator stages a sustained involuntary exposure of the Princess's secret passion, ending in a physically compromising scene where she blushes and surrenders the incriminating letter, so that the malicious gossip he had first dismissed as absurd is confirmed at her expense.

appraisal_events.evidence: His supposedly clever denials « ôtait leurs derniers doutes sur lui aux uns, inspirait leurs premiers à ceux qui n'en avaient pas encore »; Basin's tenderness is glossed as « on donne du sucre à un chien qui a fait le beau »; yet his « énorme situation » stands and the duke would « fermer les yeux » and even « prêter la main » in hope of his support.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator lowers Charlus by exposing him as a self-betraying culprit whose concealment advertises the very thing it hides, while at the same time affirming that his worldly position is untouched and that his brother courts and would protect him; the diminishment is thus of appraisal, not of standing.

status_effects.explanation: She loses all leverage locally: her hidden love is read off her face, her words, and finally a letter she must hand to the narrator, leaving her visibly compromised before a witness.
The malicious gossip the narrator had indignantly rejected is vindicated, so she ends the passage as the person the worldly voice said she was.
The narrator's analysis makes his self-defensive cleverness the instrument of his own betrayal and frames him throughout as a « coupable » prolonging a perilous conversation.
Within the same scene he is called a man of immense value, reported charming by Mme de Surgis, embraced by his brother, and credited with an « énorme situation » that the duke needs and will protect.

ambiguities: The duke's tenderness toward Charlus is left explicitly undecidable by the text (« soit qu'il eût en effet peine à la contenir, soit pour que le baron se souvînt... »), so it is recorded as a qualifying element of the mixed Charlus event rather than as an independent act of family praise.

Charlus's local movement is genuinely double-edged: the passage simultaneously discredits his secret and confirms his social invulnerability, which is why one mixed event with opposed status dimensions is preferred to two competing events.
